rows.title: Arran brown
rows.evidence: The English name comes from the original record on the Isle of Arran in 1803. The same paragraph says it is questionable whether the butterfly occurs in the British Isles.
rows.summary: It is questionable whether this butterfly occurs in the British Isles but historical collections of the Scotch argus (Erebia aethiops) contain some specimens of Arran brown among the very similar specimens of Scottish argus. The original record is from the Isle of Arran, in the Clyde Isles in Scotland, in 1803, and it is from this that the butterfly gets its English name.

rows.title: Spotted rock-rose
rows.evidence: The species article says the best-known of the patchy populations on the west coasts of Ireland and Wales is on Holyhead Mountain in Anglesey, and that Plantlife chose it as the county flower of Anglesey in 2002.
rows.summary: Tuberaria guttata is widely distributed in the Mediterranean region, and has a continuous distribution along the French Atlantic coast as far as the Channel Islands. Further north, its distribution is very patchy, being confined to a few localities on the west coasts of Ireland and Wales. The best-known of these populations is on the slopes of Holyhead Mountain in Anglesey. These British populations mark the northernmost limit of the species' distribution. Tuberaria guttata was chosen by Plantlife as the county flower of Anglesey in 2002.

rows.title: Black rat
rows.evidence: The Lambay Island article says Ireland's only self-sustaining long-term population of the black rat is there. The black rat is introduced; the claim is that this is the only such population in Ireland.
rows.summary: Lambay Island (Irish: Reachrainn), often simply Lambay, is an island in the Irish Sea off the coast of north County Dublin, Ireland. The island has a substantial population of rabbits. Ireland's most common rodent, the brown rat is present, as is Ireland's only self-sustaining long-term population of the black rat, with the presence of the former keeping the numbers of the latter under control.

rows.island_name: Monach Islands (Ceann Iar, Ceann Ear, Shivinish + Stockay, Shillay)
rows.title: Grey seal
rows.evidence: The Monach Islands article says the islands are of special interest for their grey seal population. The next sentence calls the colony one of the largest in the world. That sentence also gives a count and an autumn timing, which are not stored.
rows.reject_reason: The summary says the Monach Islands are of special interest for their grey seal population. It does not call the colony a principal stronghold, and the grey seal is not endemic or named for the islands. The next sentence in the article calls it one of the largest colonies, but that sentence also gives a count of seals coming ashore, which must not be stored.
rows.summary: The Monach Islands, also known as Heisker, are an island group west of North Uist in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland. The islands are of special interest for undisturbed machair and their grey seal population.

rows.title: Northern gannet
rows.evidence: The Sula Sgeir article says the island is best known for its population of gannets, and that the name is from Old Norse súla, gannet, and sker, skerry. A later sentence gives a breeding-pair count, and the guga-hunt section gives quotas and methods. Neither is stored.
rows.reject_reason: The article says Sula Sgeir is best known for gannets and that the island's name means gannet skerry. The northern gannet is not endemic, not named for the island, and the article does not call this colony a principal stronghold. A breeding-pair count appears later in the article and must not be stored.
rows.summary: Sula Sgeir is a small, uninhabited Scottish islet in the North Atlantic, 18 kilometres (9+1⁄2 nautical miles) west of Rona. One of the most remote islands of the British Isles, it lies approximately forty nautical miles (seventy kilometres) north of Lewis and is best known for its population of gannets. The modern name is from the Old Norse súla, "gannet" and sker, "skerry".
